mainEntity.name: How accurate is the U.S. Navy body fat method?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's generally accurate within a few percentage points for most people, making it a solid free alternative to calipers or scans, though not as precise as DEXA or hydrostatic testing.

mainEntity.name: Why does the formula differ for men and women?

acceptedAnswer.text: Body fat distribution patterns differ by sex, so the formula includes hip measurement for women to account for typical fat distribution differences.

mainEntity.name: What is a healthy body fat percentage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ranges vary, but roughly 10-20% for men and 18-28% for women are commonly cited as healthy ranges, with athletic ranges running lower — exact healthy ranges vary by age and individual factors.

mainEntity.name: How often should I re-measure my body fat?

acceptedAnswer.text: Monthly is a reasonable cadence for tracking meaningful change — body fat percentage doesn't shift dramatically week to week, so frequent measurement mostly captures measurement noise rather than real change.

mainEntity.name: How does the Navy method compare to a DEXA scan?

acceptedAnswer.text: DEXA scans are generally considered more accurate, but the Navy circumference method is a reasonably close, free alternative for most people, typically within a few percentage points.

mainEntity.name: Where exactly should I measure my waist and neck?

acceptedAnswer.text: Waist is typically measured at the navel level, and neck just below the larynx — consistent placement each time you measure matters more than the exact spot, for tracking change over time.

mainEntity.name: Tape measure or skinfold calipers — which is better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both are estimates. Skinfolds taken by a trained person can be quite accurate, but results vary a lot with technique; the tape method is easier to repeat consistently at home. Pick one and use it the same way each time.
